CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13: the list of compromised remote controllers now includes Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb besides Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, campaigns against these devices are probably still ongoing, and an unpatched end-of-life unit kept on the internet is very likely to be compromised, so a factory reset alone is insufficient (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). NCSC Switzerland published advisory 13054 on 2026-10-13 with the exploitation status Actively Exploited. It lists the Danfoss AK-SM 800 (end of life, no longer patched), the AK-SC 355 (phased out, no longer patched) and the current AK-SM 800A series when it runs outdated firmware, says no fixes exist for the two older models and that Danfoss urges replacing them, and says the attack could affect other sectors, such as healthcare for specialized cooling equipment, so organisations should check whether affected devices are in use (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told Cooling Post that the AK-SM800 was declared end of life in 2021, that the AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016, and that the affected AK-SM800A systems ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12). Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss refrigeration systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted, and that Aldi, Lidl and Coop say they are not affected (Blick, 2026-10-13); no source reports a Swiss victim. The advisory relays a six-step CERT-FR sequence (limit access to trusted addresses, factory reset, apply all fixes, rotate passwords and secrets, review accounts, reconfigure) and lists filtering to trusted addresses as a temporary measure (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), whereas the revised CERT-FR page puts removal of internet exposure first, accepts source-address filtering only as an emergency stop-gap and lists no secret rotation or account review (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

item.title: Update: GitLab's CVSS 10.0 CI regex flaw now has a public PoC; the demonstrated path needs push access to a public project
item.description: Rapid7 reported on 2026-10-13 that it reproduced arbitrary code execution on GitLab CE 19.4.1, published a proof of concept, and found no confirmed exploitation in the wild. The demonstrated path needs push access to a public project and then an unauthenticated CI lint request, so instances with open sign-up or public projects that untrusted users can write to are the exposed case.
item.content:encoded:
Update14 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Rapid7 reported on 2026-10-13 that it reproduced arbitrary code execution on GitLab CE 19.4.1, published a proof of concept, and found no confirmed exploitation in the wild. The demonstrated path needs push access to a public project and then an unauthenticated CI lint request, so instances with open sign-up or public projects that untrusted users can write to are the exposed case.

Rapid7 reports that it independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on the official GitLab CE 19.4.1 image with address space layout randomization enabled, that the same input did not execute on the patched 19.4.2 image, and that it found no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Its testing shows the unauthenticated label needs a qualifier: the attacker must first push a malicious CI/CD configuration and a UTF-8 repository path to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do where users may create public projects (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the proof of concept then triggers it with a request without credentials (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A proof of concept went public the same day; its README says the included offsets were tested only against the 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image, that other builds need adjusted offsets, and that the generated payload is slightly larger than 2 GiB, needing about 9 GiB of memory on the test host (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). The affected and fixed versions are unchanged.

Open finding: CVE-2026-97229, GitLab CE/EE: an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler allows code execution on self-managed servers and now has a public proof of concept; fixed in 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8, and 19.4.1 does not close it (CVSS 10.0) →

item.title: German portal vendor reports an exploited zero-day and calls it AI-driven; police neither confirm nor deny that
item.description: Innocon, the Tangermünde developer of the "digitales Rathaus" citizen portal, said in an MDR report of 2026-10-13 that attackers found and exploited a vulnerability it did not know of in its software, run for Tangerhütte on systems of the state municipal IT provider KID; the portal was taken offline in September and four more communes pulled theirs as a precaution. Innocon says the attackers reached only test accounts and took no real data, and classifies the intrusion as AI-driven because of command speed and on-host tool development, which is the vendor's reading: the state criminal police can neither confirm nor deny it. No CVE, product version or fix is named.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB3

Tangerhütte (Saxony-Anhalt): the vendor of the municipal citizen-portal software says attackers exploited a zero-day in it, classifies the intrusion as AI-driven, and four other communes took their portals offline

MDR AKTUELL reports on 2026-10-13 that the vendor of Tangerhütte's "digitales Rathaus" citizen portal says attackers found and exploited a vulnerability in its software that the vendor did not know of and for which no security update existed (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). The portal, an app-based service that went online in 2020, was taken offline in September, and MDR Sachsen-Anhalt reported on 2026-09-16 that the municipality said it had repelled an attack and gave no technical detail (MDR Sachsen-Anhalt, 2026-09-16). The software runs on systems that the state municipal IT provider KID operates for Tangerhütte; an IT employee noticed irregularities in the morning after the attack began at night, the server was isolated and cut from the internet, and the vendor analysed the secured logs on an offline notebook (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). Innocon told other affected communes, four of which also took their portals offline as a precaution although there was no sign of an attack on them, and says the attackers reached only test accounts and took no real data (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). Citizens could use the services only on paper for weeks (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13).

The vendor classifies the intrusion as AI-driven for two reasons: commands were executed faster than copy-and-paste would allow, and the follow-on steps were not prepared in advance but developed on the city's server during the attack, whereas human attackers normally upload their own code and do not change it (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). That is the vendor's reading of its own logs. The state criminal police are investigating data espionage and can neither confirm nor deny an AI attack, and two professors told MDR the reading is plausible without having seen the logs (MDR AKTUELL, 2026-10-13). No CVE, product version, fixed release or entry vector is named.

Exposure
Municipalities running Innocon's digitales Rathaus, which is used for Tangerhütte and at least four further communes that Innocon informed; whether any Swiss body runs it is not reported. The case matters to communal administrations as a supplier-built citizen portal hosted by a shared municipal IT provider, where the customer cannot patch an unknown flaw itself.
Detection
The vendor's two observations are the pattern to look for in a portal host's logs: commands issued faster than a person could type them, and follow-on scripts written and run on the host within the same session rather than uploaded once.
Defender takeaway
For a citizen portal built on a supplier's software, an exploited unknown flaw leaves isolation as the only lever, and this case shows what worked: isolate the server, copy the logs and analyse them offline, and have the supplier warn its other customers, four of which pulled their portals as a precaution.

item.title: Adobe fixes unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 flaws in ColdFusion, Experience Manager and Commerce; no exploitation known
item.description: Adobe's 2026-10-13 bulletins fix five unauthenticated network flaws at CVSS 9.0 to 10.0 in ColdFusion 2025 and 2023 (fixed in 2025.0.14 and 2023.0.26), three unauthenticated CVSS 10.0 code-execution flaws in Experience Manager (Cloud Service 2026.9.28386 or per-issue hotfixes) and two code-execution flaws (CVSS 10.0 and 9.8) in Adobe Commerce and Magento Open Source (2026-oct builds). Adobe says it knows of no exploitation of any of them; each needs no account, so exposure rather than exploitation status decides the order. Sansec reproduced four code-execution routes for the Commerce flaw CVE-2026-103849 within 24 hours of the fix, sees no exploitation yet, and warns that a Composer install keeps the vulnerable base version until the 2026-oct release or Adobe's isolated patch is applied.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-105899 +9updatedNATOA2

Adobe October 2026 bulletins: unauthenticated CVSS 9.0 to 10.0 flaws, most leading to code execution, in ColdFusion (APSB26-144), Experience Manager (APSB26-152) and Commerce and Magento (APSB26-153), none reported exploited

Adobe's 2026-10-13 bulletins put critical fixes into three server products: ColdFusion, Experience Manager and Commerce. Adobe says it is not aware of any exploits in the wild for the ColdFusion issues (Adobe ColdFusion APSB26-144, 2026-10-13). ColdFusion 2025 up to 2025.0.13 and 2023 up to 2023.0.25 are affected and 2025.0.14 and 2023.0.26 fix them; the bulletin lists five network flaws that need no privileges at CVSS 9.0 or above: an unrestricted file upload leading to arbitrary code execution (CVE-2026-105899, 10.0), a server-side request forgery rated privilege escalation (CVE-2026-106622, 10.0), an input-validation flaw leading to code execution (CVE-2026-106624, 9.8), a code injection rated privilege escalation (CVE-2026-106621, 9.1) and a further input-validation code-execution flaw (CVE-2026-106619, 9.0, high complexity), besides code-execution flaws that need a low-privileged account at 9.9 (Adobe ColdFusion APSB26-144, 2026-10-13).

Experience Manager APSB26-152 covers Cloud Service 2026.9.28187 and earlier, 6.5 up to Service Pack 25 and 6.5 LTS up to Service Pack 3: three incorrect-authorization flaws that lead to arbitrary code execution are scored 10.0 with no privileges required (CVE-2026-90532, CVE-2026-48383, CVE-2026-48382), fixed by Cloud Service 2026.9.28386 and, on 6.5 and 6.5 LTS, by per-issue hotfixes, and Adobe is not aware of exploits of these either (Adobe Experience Manager APSB26-152, 2026-10-13). Commerce and Magento APSB26-153 fixes a template-engine injection leading to code execution (CVE-2026-103849, 10.0, which Adobe marks as needing no authentication) and an incorrect-authorization code-execution flaw (CVE-2026-92909, 9.8, which Adobe's note tags B2B) in builds up to the 2026-sep release; the fixes are the 2026-oct builds, Adobe Commerce B2B has its own 2026-oct builds, Magento Open Source gets them for 2.4.9, 2.4.8 and 2.4.7, and Adobe asks customers to apply the CVE-2026-75650 hotfix from its September APSB26-146 update as well, and Adobe is likewise not aware of exploits (Adobe Commerce APSB26-153, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
ColdFusion 2025 and 2023, Experience Manager Cloud Service, 6.5 and 6.5 LTS, and Adobe Commerce or Magento Open Source 2.4.x that untrusted networks can reach; none of the flaws named by CVE id above needs an account.
Detection
Adobe publishes no exploit behavior. As an inference from the flaw classes: after unexpected requests to upload or administrative endpoints, look for new script files in web-accessible directories (the upload flaw), and for outbound requests from the application server to internal addresses (the request forgery).
Defender takeaway
Update internet-facing ColdFusion, Experience Manager and Commerce or Magento instances first, because the flaws need no login and the order is set by exposure; Adobe reports no exploitation as of 2026-10-13. A Composer-installed Commerce or Magento store needs the 2026-oct release or Adobe's isolated patch applied explicitly (Sansec, 2026-10-15).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:13 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidenceverificationsourcing_noteactionsbody

Sansec reports that it reproduced four different attack routes to code execution for the Commerce and Magento template-engine flaw CVE-2026-103849 within 24 hours of Adobe's fix and expects threat actors to do the same, and that it has not seen attacks on live stores (Sansec, 2026-10-15). It describes the flaw as a second-pass directive injection like September's StyleSmuggler, where attacker-controlled data in a child template can still be signed and re-scanned at the root level so that a smuggled block directive runs inside Magento's rendering, and says Adobe's October patch replaces that generic re-scan with registered placeholders (Sansec, 2026-10-15). Sansec questions Adobe's priority 2 rating for the Commerce bulletin, a 30-day patch window, because StyleSmuggler went from a priority 1 hotfix to mass exploitation in three days and it judges BlockStrap to be of similar complexity (Sansec, 2026-10-15).

Two cautions for the patch: a plain Composer install still has the vulnerable base version, so the 2026-oct release or Adobe's isolated patch must be applied, and BlockStrap and StyleSmuggler are separate fixes, so the September hotfix for CVE-2026-75650 has to stay in place as well (Sansec, 2026-10-15). Sansec lists Adobe Commerce up to 2.4.9, Adobe Commerce B2B up to 1.5.3 and Magento Open Source up to 2.4.9 as affected (Sansec, 2026-10-15).

item.title: Exchange October updates fix an unauthenticated email-borne RCE; 2016 and 2019 get their last update, and only with ESU
item.description: Microsoft's 2026-10-13 Exchange security updates fix CVE-2026-70571, a stack-based buffer overflow that an unauthenticated attacker can trigger with a crafted email (Critical, CVSS 8.1 with high attack complexity, Exploitation More Likely, not exploited), and CVE-2026-70279, a 9.3 cross-site scripting flaw that lets an attacker act as an administrator who clicks a crafted link. October is the last month Exchange 2016 and 2019 customers enrolled in the Period 2 ESU receive newly released updates, and organisations without ESU have no 2016 or 2019 update at all. Microsoft's Exchange Team says the October Windows Server updates (KB5126646, KB5126655, KB5126651, KB5126868) can make Exchange servers unstable, with OWA failures, growing mail queues and lost DAG quorum, whether or not the Exchange update is installed; it advises against uninstalling them and on 2026-10-17 gave a registry workaround.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-70571 +1updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-70571, Microsoft Exchange Server: an unauthenticated crafted-email code-execution flaw in the October 2026 security updates, the last Exchange 2016 and 2019 updates under the paid ESU (CVSS 8.1)

Microsoft's October 2026 Exchange security updates, released on 2026-10-13, fix CVE-2026-70571, a stack-based buffer overflow in Exchange Server: an unauthenticated attacker could send a specially crafted email to an affected server, triggering an internal content-conversion process, with no user interaction (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Microsoft rates it Critical (CVSS 8.1, high attack complexity) and Exploitation More Likely, and says exploitation requires a deep understanding of the target environment and is not guaranteed to succeed (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). CVE-2026-70279 is a cross-site scripting spoofing flaw (CVSS 9.3, also Exploitation More Likely): an attacker who persuades an administrator to click a crafted link could act with that administrator's privileges (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Microsoft lists neither as exploited or publicly disclosed, and no other source reports exploitation.

The fixed builds are Exchange Server Subscription Edition RTM 15.02.2562.056, 2019 CU15 15.02.1748.055, 2019 CU14 15.02.1544.050 and 2016 CU23 15.01.2507.077 (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). The 2016 and 2019 updates are available only to organisations enrolled in the Period 2 ESU program, and October 2026 is the last month those customers receive newly released updates (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13). After October, updates ship for Subscription Edition only, Microsoft's announcements and CVEs stop mentioning 2016 and 2019, and Microsoft says that does not mean those versions are not vulnerable and that it will stop testing them for vulnerabilities (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13); buying Period 2 ESU later only gets an organisation current through this release (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13). Exchange Online customers are already protected (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
On-premises Exchange Subscription Edition, 2019 CU14 and CU15 and 2016 CU23 that receive external mail for CVE-2026-70571, and administrator sessions in the web interfaces for CVE-2026-70279. The update also has to go onto machines that only run the Exchange Management Tools (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13).
Detection
No source describes exploitation behavior. Microsoft says a successful attempt is not guaranteed, so, as an inference from the mechanism, a failed attempt would more likely appear as a crash than a shell: watch for crashes and application-log faults of the Exchange transport processes right after inbound mail from outside, and for unexpected child processes of those processes.
Defender takeaway
Install the October update on every Exchange server and management-tools machine, because Microsoft rates both flaws Exploitation More Likely. An organisation still on Exchange 2016 or 2019 without Period 2 ESU has no update for CVE-2026-70571 and no further updates after this one; the choices are enrolling, which ends at October's release, or moving to Subscription Edition. On an Exchange host that also takes the October Windows Server update, do not uninstall that update: Microsoft says the OWA failures, growing mail queues and lost DAG quorum that can follow are not caused by the Exchange security update, and its workaround is to set the Rpc registry value EpmapSavedContextCap to 65536 and reboot (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-17).
Improvement16 Oct 2026 04:10 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummaryevidencebody

Microsoft's Exchange Team added a notice on 2026-10-15: it has received reports that installing the October 2026 Windows Server updates, KB5126646 (Windows Server 2025), KB5126655 (Windows Server 2022), KB5126651 (Windows Server 2019) or KB5126868 (Windows Server 2016), can make Exchange OWA fail with the error MapiExceptionMdbOffline (event ID 1006 in the Application log) and mail queues grow (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13). Microsoft says that installing the October 2026 Exchange updates is not required for the issues to occur, and that it is investigating with its Windows partners; the notice names no workaround or fix (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-13).

Update17 Oct 2026 03:36 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-intelsummarysourcesevidenceactionsbody

Microsoft's Exchange Team has published guidance for Exchange servers that become unstable after the October 2026 Windows Server updates. Since 2026-10-13 it has seen reports of OWA failing with MapiExceptionMdbOffline (hr=0x80004005, ec=1142; event ID 1006 in the Application log), mail queues growing during the day, DAG members unable to reach quorum and a reboot helping only temporarily; Exchange 2016, 2019 and Subscription Edition can all be affected (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-17). It says the issues are not related to installing the October 2026 Exchange security updates and that any Exchange version running on an affected Windows build can be hit; KB5126646 (Windows Server 2025), KB5126655 (2022), KB5126651 (2019) and KB5126868 (2016) can cause the failures after some time, and the impact varies with Exchange load, so some servers may never see a problem (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-17).

Microsoft's recommendation is not to uninstall the October 2026 Windows Server updates and, from an elevated command prompt on the Exchange server, to set the registry value EpmapSavedContextCap (REG_DWORD) under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Rpc to 65536, reboot, monitor, and raise the limit if the problem recurs; it says this has solved the customer cases it has assisted (Microsoft Exchange Team, 2026-10-17).

item.title: Microsoft patches an exploited Windows Shell zero-day that evades Mark of the Web protections on files and links
item.description: Microsoft's 2026-10-13 updates fix CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell flaw that lets an attacker evade Mark of the Web defenses once a user opens a crafted file or link sent by email or instant message, so Windows does not show the dialog the tag normally triggers. Microsoft marks it exploited and CISA added it to KEV the same day; no source names the actor, the payload or the victims. Rapid7 says Windows Server 2012 gets no patch, while Microsoft lists fixes for Server 2012 R2 and every later supported release.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-96951exploitedNATOA2

CVE-2026-96951, Windows Shell: a Mark of the Web bypass exploited as a zero-day, fixed in the 2026-10-13 cumulative updates and listed in CISA KEV (CVSS 8.8)

Microsoft's 2026-10-13 release fixes CVE-2026-96951, a Windows Shell security feature bypass that Microsoft marks as exploited and not publicly disclosed (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13); CISA added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day, citing evidence of active exploitation (CISA, 2026-10-13). Microsoft says an attacker who exploits it could evade Mark of the Web defenses, by sending a crafted file by email or instant message or enticing the user to click a link or open an attachment (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Microsoft's record gives the root cause as improper neutralization of special elements in a command (command injection, CWE-77) (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 describes the effect as Windows not showing the dialog that says it protected the PC, because the tag that triggers it is bypassed, calls this the second exploited Windows Shell zero-day this year, and says the flaw also affected Outlook.com, patched in a build several weeks ago (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 says Windows Server 2012 receives no patch while Server 2012 R2 does (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and Microsoft's record lists no Windows Server 2012 product for this flaw (Microsoft Security Response Center, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2012 R2 through 2025 where users open files or links from mail, chat or the web; the fixed build per release is in the CVE record, and Rapid7 reports no patch for Windows Server 2012.
Detection
Microsoft, CISA and Rapid7 name no actor, payload or victims and no source describes the exploit's behavior, so this is a hunt hypothesis that follows from the mechanism: the failed control is the Mark of the Web tag, so there is no warning dialog for a user to report. Look at mail gateway, chat and endpoint file-origin telemetry for internet-origin files, archives and shortcuts that execute without the usual download warning, and at process lineage from explorer.exe into scripting interpreters and living-off-the-land binaries shortly after a mail or browser download.

Triage: a file a user created or received from a trusted local source also carries no tag; the discriminator is an internet origin (mail, chat or web download) together with the absence of the tag on the opened item.

Defender takeaway
Install the October cumulative update now, ahead of the monthly cycle, on endpoints that open mail and web downloads first; because the tag is the control that failed, attachment blocking and mail-gateway detonation remain the compensating layer until the update is deployed, and Rapid7 reports no patch for Windows Server 2012.

item.title: Exploited Ivanti Connect Secure chain: its root step had no fix at disclosure, and it evades the Integrity Checker
item.description: Ivanti disclosed CVE-2026-104935 on 2026-10-13, an authentication bypass in Connect Secure that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands, and says it is aware of limited exploitation; CISA listed it in KEV the same day. Volexity found a cluster it calls UTA0576 chaining it with a root escalation that Ivanti had not fixed when Volexity reported (a separate record, CVE-2026-111357, now covers that step), patching library code in memory only so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool sees no file change, and going after the appliance's Active Directory service account, LAPS passwords and BitLocker recovery keys. Fixed builds are 25.1.1.2, 25.1.3.1 and 22.8R2.5 (Rapid7 also lists 25.1.3.0, which CERT-FR counts as affected); a patched appliance that was exposed still needs a compromise check, and CERT-FR says it knows of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on the appliance and tells owners to isolate and preserve it before any reset.
item.content:encoded:
CRITICALCVE-2026-104935 +1exploitedupdatedNATOA1

CVE-2026-104935, Ivanti Connect Secure: an authentication bypass chained to code execution is exploited as a zero-day, and the root-escalation step of the chain was unpatched at disclosure (CVSS 8.6)

Ivanti disclosed a vulnerability in limited versions of Connect Secure on 2026-10-13 and says it is aware of limited exploitation in the wild (Ivanti, 2026-10-13). Rapid7 describes CVE-2026-104935 as an authentication bypass by spoofing that lets a remote unauthenticated attacker run commands, and scores it CVSS 8.6 (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). CISA added CVE-2026-104935 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day (CISA, 2026-10-13). Volexity found the activity on 2026-10-05, tracks the operator as UTA0576, a previously unknown cluster it assesses with low confidence as criminal, and dates exploitation of a fully patched 22.8R2.4 appliance to 2026-10-03 (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The chain has three steps. A request to the public login script welcome.cgi names a protected script in an X-DSCGI-PATH header, so the URL passes the authentication check while the header picks the destination. The upload script wu.cgi writes a file to disk before checking that it is a ZIP, and parallel requests run a Perl script before it is deleted. A root escalation then abuses the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache configuration store (Volexity, 2026-10-13). Ivanti tracks the first two steps under CVE-2026-104935 and, according to Volexity on 2026-10-13, had not fixed the root escalation, which it said would ship in a future release in the coming weeks (Volexity, 2026-10-13); that step now has its own identifier, CVE-2026-111357 (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15). Every command re-runs the whole chain through HTTP requests with no web shell or backdoor, and the exploit patches library code in memory only, so Ivanti's Integrity Checker Tool, which looks for file changes, does not detect it; Volexity also found entries removed from the debug and audit logs (Volexity, 2026-10-13). The operator then went after the Active Directory service account stored on the appliance: LDAP queries for LAPS passwords, BitLocker recovery keys and password attributes, a Kerberoast-capable tool, password spraying, and packet capture of plaintext LDAP, HTTP Basic and NTLM traffic (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

Exposure
Connect Secure 25.1.1.1 and prior (fixed 25.1.1.2), 25.1.2.2 and prior (fixed 25.1.3.1; Rapid7 also lists 25.1.3.0 as resolved, which CERT-FR counts as affected (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14)) and 22.8R2.4 and prior (fixed 22.8R2.5) are affected, and 22.7.x and below are not (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security labels the 25.x line 25.2.2 and prior (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13). CISA says 22.8 reaches end of life on 2027-01-31 (CISA, 2026-10-13).
Detection
The appliance's own logs were tampered with, so start upstream: web proxy, load balancer or WAF logs for many requests to welcome.cgi, above all with an X-DSCGI-PATH header (the login page itself is ordinary) or one whose script differs from the URL path. On domain controllers, look for LDAP queries from the appliance's service account for LAPS, BitLocker recovery and password-bearing attributes, Kerberos activity and spraying from the appliance's address. Volexity names a hidden directory under the appliance's /data partition holding a renamed capture binary, and post-exploitation files in /tmp, says a clean Integrity Checker result does not show the appliance is safe, and advises network and memory forensics; patching does not evict an attacker who is already in.
Defender takeaway
Upgrade now, then treat every appliance that was exposed on an affected build as a compromise-assessment target and rotate what it could reach: the root-escalation step had no fix when Volexity reported and the Integrity Checker cannot clear it. Where compromise cannot be excluded, isolate the appliance and preserve its memory and logs before any reset, because CERT-FR knows of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on it (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). CISA's recovery sequence for a suspected compromise: back up the configuration, factory-reset and upgrade (rebuild cloud and virtual appliances), restore, then reset passwords, certificates, API keys and licence-server credentials (CISA, 2026-10-13).
Update16 Oct 2026 04:10 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-intelsummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

CERT-FR's alert of 2026-10-14 says Ivanti reports the vulnerability as actively exploited and that CERT-FR itself is aware of lateral movement using the LDAP and Active Directory secrets stored on the appliance (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). It puts the response in an order: fully isolate the appliance from both the internet and the internal network, snapshot the file system and memory of a virtual appliance, avoid powering it off so that traces survive, place the logs under seal and analyse the appliance with the Volexity indicators, and only then, on compromise, factory-reset it, upgrade and reset the secrets (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its list of secrets to treat as compromised is wider than a password reset: the LDAP and Active Directory secrets, every certificate on the appliance (machine, user-authentication, code-signing and the TLS certificate of the exposed interface), the administration password, stored API keys, the passwords of local accounts including the service accounts used for authentication servers, the Kerberos tickets and other authentication material of those service accounts, and the licence-server authentication (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). CERT-FR adds that running Ivanti's external Integrity Checker Tool needs physical access to the appliance and can interrupt service, and that some threats survive a factory reset (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14). Its affected-systems list names the 22.8Rx builds before 22.8R2.5, the 25.1.1.x builds before 25.1.1.2 and the 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 and does not list a 25.1.2.x line; by counting 25.1.3.x builds before 25.1.3.1 as affected it includes 25.1.3.0, a build that Rapid7's table lists as resolved (CERT-FR, 2026-10-14).

Improvement17 Oct 2026 03:34 UTCrun 2026-10-17T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryimmediate_actioncvessourcesevidencebody

The root-escalation step of the chain now has its own identifier, CVE-2026-111357, published on 2026-10-15 and rated High on GitHub's advisory database as GHSA-fhw5-mpvj-x89m (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15). Its description reads "Ivanti Connect Secure 22.8R2.4 mishandles the manner in which the dsinvoked broker trusts DSCache configuration data, leading to privilege escalation to root, as exploited in the wild in October 2026." (GitHub Advisory Database, 2026-10-15), the same step Volexity describes as abusing the dsinvoked service's trust in the shared DSCache store (Volexity, 2026-10-13).

The record names only 22.8R2.4 as affected and states no fixed build; Volexity wrote that Ivanti was working on a fix for release in the coming weeks (Volexity, 2026-10-13), and no source read says whether any build now fixes it. The Canadian Cyber Centre's bulletin on the Ivanti advisory, updated 2026-10-16, adds that open-source reporting indicates CVE-2026-111357 is being exploited in the wild (Canadian Centre for Cyber Security, 2026-10-13). item.title: GitLab's CVSS 10.0 CI regex flaw now has a public PoC; the demonstrated path needs push access to a public project
item.description: GitLab's critical patch release of 2026-10-12 fixes CVE-2026-97229 (CVSS 3.1 10.0), an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler that lets code run on the server as the git user through a crafted expression in a CI/CD configuration; Rapid7 reported on 2026-10-13 that it reproduced it on 19.4.1 and published a proof of concept, and reports no confirmed exploitation in the wild. The demonstrated path needs push access to a public project (an ordinary account where users may create public projects), followed by a request to the CI lint API that carries no credentials. Self-managed CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5 and 19.4 before 19.4.2 are affected, and NCSC Switzerland and CERT-EU both published advisories on 2026-10-12.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHCVE-2026-97229updatedNATOA2

CVE-2026-97229, GitLab CE/EE: an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler allows code execution on self-managed servers and now has a public proof of concept; fixed in 19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8, and 19.4.1 does not close it (CVSS 10.0)

GitLab's critical patch release of 2026-10-12 (19.4.2, 19.3.5 and 19.2.8) fixes CVE-2026-97229, an integer overflow in the CI/CD regular-expression compiler that, "under certain conditions", could allow an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server through a specially crafted regular expression in a CI/CD configuration; GitLab scores it CVSS 3.1 10.0 with no privileges required (GitLab, 2026-10-12). Affected are self-managed CE and EE from 19.2 before 19.2.8, 19.3 before 19.3.5 and 19.4 before 19.4.2; GitLab.com already runs the patched version and Dedicated customers need no action (GitLab, 2026-10-12). CERT-EU and BleepingComputer give 19.3.4 as the 19.3 fix, but GitLab's page names 19.3.5 and says 19.3.4 had a merge-request page bug, so the GitLab figure governs (CERT-EU, 2026-10-12; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12). The 19.4.1 release of 2026-09-23 fixed two flaws from the same reporter in the same component, a double free in the regular-expression parser and an integer overflow in the compiler, both rated for an authenticated user (GitLab, 2026-09-23); CVE-2026-97229 is rated without that requirement, and 19.4.1 is still affected. NCSC Switzerland and CERT-EU both published advisories on 2026-10-12 (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12; CERT-EU, 2026-10-12); NCSC lists the exploitation status as unknown (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12); Rapid7 reproduced the code execution on 19.4.1, published a proof of concept, and reports no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). GitLab publishes the issue detail for a security fix 90 days after the release that carries it (GitLab, 2026-10-12).

Exposure
Self-managed GitLab CE or EE on 19.2.x below 19.2.8, 19.3.x below 19.3.5 or 19.4.x below 19.4.2; GitLab's table starts at 19.2 and lists no earlier branch (GitLab, 2026-10-12). NCSC Switzerland states the prerequisites as network access to the instance and delivery of a crafted regular expression through CI/CD configuration (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-12); Rapid7 found the conditions: an attacker must first commit a malicious CI/CD configuration file and a repository path containing UTF-8 characters to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do by creating a public project where the instance allows it (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and on instances where new users can self-register and create projects that constraint is removed (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). An instance with open sign-up, or with public projects that untrusted users can write to, is the case to prioritise.
Detection
GitLab and NCSC publish no indicators, so this is a hunt for the mechanism: in process-creation telemetry, shells, interpreters or network tools started as children of the GitLab application server processes, and in GitLab's audit and application logs, recently created or changed CI/CD configurations that carry unusual regular expressions, from accounts or addresses that have not used the instance before. Rapid7's proof of concept delivers the code through the public CI lint API without credentials, after pushing to a public project (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13): look for unauthenticated GET requests to /api/v4/projects/:id/ci/lint against a project that an account has just pushed to, and for application worker crashes that follow them, which the README says end the request with HTTP 502 while the worker is replaced (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A server where that turns up needs its CI/CD variables, runner registration tokens and deploy keys treated as exposed.

Triage: ordinary CI jobs run shells under the runners; only a shell spawned by the GitLab application server processes themselves matches this flaw, not one started inside a runner job; an anonymous CI lint request is ordinary on its own, and the signal is one aimed at a project that a newly created or little-used account has just pushed a CI configuration to.

Defender takeaway
Upgrade to 19.4.2, 19.3.5 or 19.2.8 now, starting with internet-facing instances as CERT-EU advises (CERT-EU, 2026-10-12); GitLab's release page lists no workaround as of 2026-10-13 (GitLab, 2026-10-12), Rapid7's interim controls (restrict anonymous access to public projects and stop untrusted users creating or writing to public projects) reduce exposure only to the path it demonstrated and do not fix the compiler flaw (Rapid7, 2026-10-13), and the proof of concept is tuned to one build while its author says analysis of additional reachable paths is ongoing (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13), so an instance that cannot be upgraded this week should be kept off untrusted networks; on a single-node instance the upgrade causes downtime, because migrations must finish before GitLab can start, so schedule the window now (GitLab, 2026-10-12).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:43 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytagscvessourcesevidencesourcing_noteactionsbody

Rapid7 reports that it independently reproduced arbitrary code execution on the official GitLab CE 19.4.1 image with address space layout randomization enabled, that the same input did not execute on the patched 19.4.2 image, and that it found no confirmed exploitation in the wild (Rapid7, 2026-10-13). Its testing shows the unauthenticated label needs a qualifier: the attacker must first push a malicious CI/CD configuration and a UTF-8 repository path to a branch in a public project, which an ordinary account can do where users may create public projects (Rapid7, 2026-10-13); the proof of concept then triggers it with a request without credentials (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). A proof of concept went public the same day; its README says the included offsets were tested only against the 19.4.1 CE Linux amd64 image, that other builds need adjusted offsets, and that the generated payload is slightly larger than 2 GiB, needing about 9 GiB of memory on the test host (Rapid7 proof-of-concept README, 2026-10-13). The affected and fixed versions are unchanged.

item.title: CERT-FR adds Copeland and Dixell xweb to the hijacked refrigeration controllers; NCSC.ch rates the attacks exploited
item.description: Coopérative U, Intermarché and E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems overnight on 11 to 12 October 2026, which BFMTV reports as a remotely forced defrost at hundreds of stores. CERT-FR's alert, revised on 2026-10-13, reports numerous compromises of Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC controllers and now also of Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, says campaigns are probably still running and that a factory reset alone does not protect an unpatched end-of-life unit, and NCSC Switzerland rates the activity actively exploited. Danfoss says most affected units are legacy products or current AK-SM800A units on outdated firmware; no source names an actor, the flaw or how the attackers got in, and the Paris prosecutor is investigating.
item.content:encoded:
HIGHexploitedupdatedNATOA2

Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb refrigeration controllers compromised, with forced defrost reported at hundreds of French supermarkets; CERT-FR and NCSC Switzerland say to remove internet exposure

Coopérative U, Intermarché and E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP a cyberattack on their refrigeration systems overnight on 11 to 12 October 2026; AFP reports from the retailers' statements at least 300 Intermarché or Netto shops and more than 100 Coopérative U outlets, and the Paris prosecutor opened an investigation (AFP, 2026-10-12). BFMTV puts the Intermarché and Netto count at 300, which it says is twice the first estimates of 150 points of sale, and Coopérative U below 100 stores, while Infosecurity quotes 150 Intermarché and 30 Netto stores (BFMTV, 2026-10-12; Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12). BFMTV, writing in the conditional, reports that the attackers are said to have imposed a forced, continuous defrost with the setpoint at 50 degrees, on software older than version 4, heating the equipment for hours (translated from French) (BFMTV, 2026-10-12). CERT-FR's alert, in its revision of 2026-10-13, says it knows of numerous compromises of the remote refrigeration controllers Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC series as well as Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb, and that exposing a management interface to the internet is contrary to good practice (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told AFP that most affected units are legacy products that no longer receive software or security updates, naming the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 regulators, and a person close to the Prime Minister said ANSSI had identified a vulnerability in software from a Danish company and that other countries may be affected (AFP, 2026-10-12). Intermarché told BleepingComputer that the attack reportedly affected a service provider that manages refrigeration systems in stores (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12), and E. Leclerc told AFP that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers (AFP, 2026-10-12). Infosecurity says the affected stores include those running vulnerable consoles with remote control and no adequately secured communication channel (Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12). No source names an actor or the flaw or states how the attackers got in, and none confirms a tie to the 2025 AK-SM 8xxA vulnerabilities that Claroty found: BleepingComputer reports no tie (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-12) and NCSC Switzerland lists three of them only as alleged to be potentially related (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13); Censys names the same three as flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier and says Danfoss has not confirmed the initial access vector (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Exposure
A Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC refrigeration controller, or a Copeland or Dixell xweb unit, whose management interface is reachable from the internet, above all legacy units; Danfoss says the current AK-SM800A units that were affected ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12), and CERT-FR names no models, flaw or entry vector for the Copeland and Dixell units (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). Infosecurity reports, without naming them, that supermarkets in Belgium and the Netherlands were also reportedly affected (Infosecurity Magazine, 2026-10-12); Blick reports that Migros confirms using, in a limited number of its Swiss stores, the same Danfoss refrigeration systems that were targeted and says nothing indicates an attack on them, while Aldi and Lidl say they are not concerned and Coop says it was not affected and declines to say whether it uses Danfoss (Blick, 2026-10-13); no source reports a Swiss victim, so ask whoever manages your refrigeration and building services whether a controller sits in your estate. For an AK-SM 800A, Censys maps the firmware to the published flaws: a build below 4.2 carries all three, 4.2.4 fixes only the date-based login and so still carries the two later ones, and 4.3.1 or later fixes all three, with 5.3.2 the current build it lists (Censys, 2026-10-14).
Detection
On the controller, defrost, setpoint and account changes outside a maintenance window; in firewall, provider VPN or ISP logs, inbound connections to the management interface from addresses other than the refrigeration contractor's; CERT-FR accepts filtering to the contractors' source addresses only as an emergency measure and wants access restored through a secure VPN or protected network (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). For a controller that may have been taken over, CERT-FR's sequence is to remove the internet exposure, factory-reset the unit, restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network, reconfigure it and apply the maker's practices, which for Danfoss means updating the firmware, setting the security level to Strict and confirming the default passwords were changed (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

Triage: a defrost cycle is normal; BFMTV quotes sector professionals saying installations can be programmed for two hours of defrost per 24 hours, whereas the reported attack is said to be a continuous forced defrost at a 50-degree setpoint held for hours (translated from French) (BFMTV, 2026-10-12).

Defender takeaway
Take any Danfoss AK-SM or AK-SC, Copeland xweb or Dixell xweb management interface off the internet now and restore access only through a secure VPN or protected network, as CERT-FR advises (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13), and ask the contractor whether its own remote access was affected; for the AK-SM800 and AK-SC355, replacement is the lever, since Danfoss says it had long advised supermarkets to move off those models (AFP, 2026-10-12), no fix exists for them according to NCSC Switzerland (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), and CERT-FR says a factory reset on an unpatched end-of-life unit removes the implant but leaves the device vulnerable and almost certainly compromised again (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).
Update14 Oct 2026 03:44 UTCrun 2026-10-14T0255Z-inteltitleheadlinesummaryregionsentitiesaffected_productssourcesevidencesourcing_notereferencesactionsbody

CERT-FR revised its alert on 2026-10-13: the list of compromised remote controllers now includes Copeland xweb and Dixell xweb besides Danfoss AK-SM and AK-SC, campaigns against these devices are probably still ongoing, and an unpatched end-of-life unit kept on the internet is very likely to be compromised, so a factory reset alone is insufficient (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13). NCSC Switzerland published advisory 13054 on 2026-10-13 with the exploitation status Actively Exploited. It lists the Danfoss AK-SM 800 (end of life, no longer patched), the AK-SC 355 (phased out, no longer patched) and the current AK-SM 800A series when it runs outdated firmware, says no fixes exist for the two older models and that Danfoss urges replacing them, and says the attack could affect other sectors, such as healthcare for specialized cooling equipment, so organisations should check whether affected devices are in use (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13). Danfoss told Cooling Post that the AK-SM800 was declared end of life in 2021, that the AK-SC355 was phased out in 2016, and that the affected AK-SM800A systems ran outdated firmware (Cooling Post, 2026-10-12). Blick reports that Migros uses the same Danfoss refrigeration systems in a limited number of Swiss stores and sees no sign they were targeted, and that Aldi, Lidl and Coop say they are not affected (Blick, 2026-10-13); no source reports a Swiss victim. The advisory relays a six-step CERT-FR sequence (limit access to trusted addresses, factory reset, apply all fixes, rotate passwords and secrets, review accounts, reconfigure) and lists filtering to trusted addresses as a temporary measure (NCSC Switzerland, 2026-10-13), whereas the revised CERT-FR page puts removal of internet exposure first, accepts source-address filtering only as an emergency stop-gap and lists no secret rotation or account review (CERT-FR, 2026-10-13).

Improvement15 Oct 2026 03:49 UTCrun 2026-10-15T0256Z-intelsourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

Censys, which scans for Danfoss StoreView control panels, says Danfoss has not confirmed the initial access vector and points to three AK-SM 800A flaws that Danfoss patched more than a year earlier: CVE-2025-41450 (March 2025), which Censys describes as letting an unauthenticated actor log in as an administrator with a code computed from the current calendar date, and CVE-2025-41451 and CVE-2025-41452 (August 2025), which it says let authenticated users run commands and disrupt the management interface (Censys, 2026-10-14). Censys maps the firmware by build: below 4.2 carries all three, 4.2.4 fixes only the date-based login and still carries the two later ones, and 4.3.1 or later fixes all three (Censys, 2026-10-14). Its scan counted 1,825 exposed StoreView panels in France on 2026-10-11 and 537 on 2026-10-14, a fall of 71 percent, with builds below 4.2, build 4.2.4 and builds from 4.3.1 leaving at about the same rate, which it reads as operators taking controllers off the internet rather than patching them (Censys, 2026-10-14). Outside France the count fell from 1,166 to 966, and in ten of the twelve countries with the most exposed hosts more than 60 percent of the hosts run a build below 4.3.1, led by Poland at 81 percent and Romania at 80 percent (Censys, 2026-10-14).

Builds on: A hidden authentication mechanism discloses internal network layout before an attacker even… · An attacker can reconstruct admin credentials for an exposed refrigeration controller offline…

item.title: Bricksforge's Pro Forms upload flaw is exploited without login since 7 October; fixed in 4.0.1 and 3.1.8.10
item.description: Patchstack reports that CVE-2026-85097, an unauthenticated arbitrary file upload in the Pro Forms module of Bricksforge, a paid WordPress add-on for the Bricks page builder, has been targeted in the wild since 2026-10-07: it lets an attacker with no account get a PHP file written to the uploads directory and executed, on versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 with Pro Forms active (about 6,000 active installations). Bricksforge's changelog of 2026-10-08 lists the fix in 4.0.1 and Patchstack names 3.1.8.10 for the 3.x line; the exploitation report rests on Patchstack's telemetry.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLECVE-2026-85097exploitedNATOB2

CVE-2026-85097, Bricksforge for WordPress: an unauthenticated upload in the Pro Forms module writes attacker PHP into the uploads directory, exploited since 7 October; fixed in 4.0.1 and 3.1.8.10 (CVSS 9.8)

Bricksforge's Pro Forms module checks a file's type when it is first uploaded but trusts the file metadata the client sends when the form is submitted, in particular the url field of the temporaryFileUploads parameter (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). An attacker obtains a nonce from the unauthenticated bricksforge_regenerate_nonce AJAX endpoint, uploads a GIF/PHP polyglot that passes the type check, then submits a form whose file path names that image and whose url ends in a PHP extension; the plugin writes the image's content to the PHP path and one request to it executes the code (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 are affected (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). The vendor's changelog lists the fix in 4.0.1 (Bricksforge, 2026-10-08), while Patchstack names 3.1.8.10 as the fixed build of the 3.x line, which the public changelog does not list (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09). Dr. Web credits Wordfence with a CVSS score of 9.8 and Patchstack with 10.0 (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).

Patchstack's telemetry first recorded exploitation attempts on 2026-10-07 at 21:47 UTC, from 63 distinct source addresses, and it calls the activity automated without attributing it (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Patchstack describes exploitation attempts and says an attacker with execution can deploy web shells, modify site content, read data and persist (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). It counts about 6,000 active installations (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09), Previdian tags the flaw "PoC available" (Previdian, 2026-10-08), and the flaw is not in CISA's KEV catalog (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).

Exposure
WordPress sites running Bricksforge versions up to and including 3.1.8.9 (Patchstack, 2026-10-08) with the Pro Forms module active, including sites whose forms have no upload field (Bricksforge, 2026-10-08). Patchstack and Dr. Web bound the affected range at 3.1.8.9 (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09), but the vendor's upload fix ships in 4.0.1, the release after 4.0.0 of 2026-09-17, and its changelog gives no affected range, so whether 4.0.0 is affected is not stated (Bricksforge, 2026-10-08). Bricksforge is not in the wordpress.org plugin directory, so no public version statistics exist, and updates come with an annual licence, so a site with a lapsed licence may not receive the fix (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).
Detection
In web server and WordPress access logs, POST requests to /wp-json/bricksforge/v1/form_submit or to admin-ajax with the bricksforge_form_submit action that carry a temporaryFileUploads value pairing an image path with a PHP-extension destination, preceded by a call to the nonce endpoint and repeated with changing extensions, case or encodings, from 2026-10-07 onward; in file-integrity and endpoint telemetry, new PHP files in the WordPress uploads tree, the plugin's temporary upload folder first, and web requests to them (Patchstack, 2026-10-08). Patchstack says a site that ran a vulnerable version without protection should have its historical logs and the host reviewed for unexpected PHP files, unusual application activity and unauthorized changes (Patchstack, 2026-10-08); Dr. Web adds a check of the user list for unknown administrator accounts (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).
Defender takeaway
Update every Bricksforge site to 4.0.1, or to 3.1.8.10 on the 3.x line, now; where that is not possible, deactivate Pro Forms or the plugin and block PHP execution in the uploads directory (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09). On a site that was reachable and unpatched since 2026-10-07, run the log and file search above, and if code turns up restore from a backup older than 2026-10-07 and change all passwords (Dr. Web, 2026-10-09).

item.description: The abused company is Pays ApS of Odense, which confirmed it to TV 2; Politiken reports that at least three of its accounts, including the administrator account, used the password 123456, and an anonymous hacker says access began with a leaked former employee's password, a claim. item.content:encoded:
Update11 Oct 2026 03:40 UTCrun 2026-10-11T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarytechniquessourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

The abused company is Pays ApS of Odense, which confirmed it to TV 2; Politiken reports that at least three of its accounts, including the administrator account, used the password 123456, and an anonymous hacker says access began with a leaked former employee's password, a claim. Ritzau puts the access at 21 days and 17 hours from 10 September, where the minister had described about ten days.

Pays ApS, a company in Odense that had two employees as of July 2026 according to Denmark's Central Business Register, confirmed to TV 2 on 2026-10-09 that it is the company whose lawful access to search the CPR system was abused (The Copenhagen Post (Ritzau), 2026-10-10). Politiken, which reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used, reports that at least three user accounts at Pays used the password 123456, one of them the administrator account, and an Aarhus University professor called the company's password security hopeless (The Copenhagen Post (Ritzau), 2026-10-10).

An anonymous hacker told Politiken that they were behind the attack and that access was first obtained with a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company, after which they allegedly created two programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally; the article does not say that this was a Pays employee, and it is the hacker's account, not a finding (The Copenhagen Post (Ritzau), 2026-10-10). TT reports that the experts Politiken interviewed consider it likely that the hacker was involved in the breach (translated from Swedish) (TV4 Nyheterna (TT), 2026-10-08). Ritzau reports that the hacker had access from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours, which differs from the minister's earlier description of about ten days (The Copenhagen Post (Ritzau), 2026-10-10).

Open finding: Denmark's CPR population register: unauthorised parties abused a small private company's lawful lookup access, where Politiken reports at least three accounts used the password 123456, and obtained names, addresses and CPR numbers of 8.8 million people →

item.title: Update: A self-propagating npm worm reaches packages totalling 1.3 billion monthly downloads, and its C2 address lives on-chain
item.description: A further package, tensorlake@0.5.144 (the npm SDK of an AI-agent sandbox platform), was published on 2026-10-08 with a Shai-Hulud-family payload through the project's normal GitHub Actions pipeline with valid build provenance; Socket and OX Security describe the dead-man switch that wipes the owner's home directory when the stolen GitHub token is revoked, and both say to remove its persistence before revoking. Socket matches the release to this wave, while OX Security says new keys may point to an independent actor reusing the name.
item.content:encoded:
Update11 Oct 2026 03:39 UTCrun 2026-10-11T0256Z-intelactionsevidencesourcessourcing_notesummarytechniquesbody

A further package, tensorlake@0.5.144 (the npm SDK of an AI-agent sandbox platform), was published on 2026-10-08 with a Shai-Hulud-family payload through the project's normal GitHub Actions pipeline with valid build provenance; Socket and OX Security describe the dead-man switch that wipes the owner's home directory when the stolen GitHub token is revoked, and both say to remove its persistence before revoking. Socket matches the release to this wave, while OX Security says new keys may point to an independent actor reusing the name.

A further package carrying this payload family was published on 2026-10-08: tensorlake@0.5.144, the npm SDK of an AI-agent sandbox platform, went out at 01:12 UTC with a preinstall hook that runs an obfuscated loader, which in turn launches a large payload under Bun; Socket flagged it about 11 minutes later, the release has since been removed and 0.5.143 is clean (Socket, 2026-10-08; Endor Labs, 2026-10-08). Socket says the hook and payload file names match the structure documented in the August wave (Socket, 2026-10-08). Endor Labs reports that the release shipped through the project's normal GitHub Actions pipeline with valid build provenance after the attacker modified the main branch first, most likely through a compromised maintainer account, and notes that provenance confirms where a build came from, not that the source was clean (Endor Labs, 2026-10-08). That is the situation the update of 2026-08-08 warned about, now on a published package. Socket reports that the payload harvests npm and GitHub tokens, AWS credentials (instance metadata, ECS, Secrets Manager and Parameter Store), a local HashiCorp Vault, Kubernetes service-account tokens and kubeconfig files, SSH keys, environment files and AI-tool configuration, resolves its endpoint from an Ethereum contract through about 30 public RPC endpoints with a GitHub fallback, and republishes itself with Sigstore provenance to packages the victim can publish (Socket, 2026-10-08).

The dead-man switch is described in detail here. A PowerShell monitor persisted through a scheduled task that runs at logon polls the GitHub API with the stolen token and, when the token is revoked, runs an attacker-supplied handler; Socket says the revoke-wipe string in the code appeared in earlier waves (Socket, 2026-10-08). Socket and OX Security both tell responders to isolate the host and remove the gh-token-monitor persistence first (a systemd user unit on Linux, a LaunchAgent on macOS, a scheduled task on Windows) and only then revoke and rotate, because revoking while the monitor runs wipes the user's home directory; removing the npm dependency alone does not remove that persistence (Socket, 2026-10-08; OX Security, 2026-10-08).

Attribution is split: Socket frames the release as part of this wave (Socket, 2026-10-08), while OX Security reports new public keys that may indicate an independent actor or a new group using the Shai-Hulud name (OX Security, 2026-10-08).

Open finding: CHAINDROP, the Shai-Hulud npm worm returns through the keyv maintainer, backdoors 400+ packages, and resolves its exfiltration endpoint from an Ethereum smart contract →

item.title: IDCF Cloud outage: backups now retrievable for 194 of 495 customers; provider finds no trace of server data taken
item.description: IDC Frontier, a SoftBank Group subsidiary, says a ransomware attack from about 3:40 a.m. on 2026-10-07 stopped four zones of its IDCF Cloud East Japan Region 1, affecting 495 companies and local governments. Its fifth report (2026-10-14) says its backup data is safe and retrievable for the 194 affected customers that used its snapshot function, and that it found no trace of data in customers' virtual servers being queried or taken, while confirming improper queries of the portal registration data of 48 customers; the intrusion route is not public.
item.content:encoded:
ROUTINEupdatedNATOA1

IDC Frontier: ransomware stops four zones of IDCF Cloud for 495 companies and local governments; the provider now says its backups are safe and retrievable for 194 customers and that it found no trace of data taken from customers' virtual servers

IDC Frontier says a ransomware attack that began around 3:40 a.m. on 2026-10-07 stopped four zones of IDCF Cloud East Japan Region 1, affecting 495 companies and local governments, among them the websites of Ibaraki Prefecture and the city of Kodaira, and has suspended customer management consoles in every region; no source names the actor, the ransomware family or the intrusion route (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-07; IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08; BleepingComputer, 2026-10-08; Jiji Press via nippon.com, 2026-10-07). The lesson is supplier concentration: local governments sat behind one provider whose recovery first depended on copies the customers held, until the fifth report made the provider's own snapshot backups retrievable for 194 of the 495.

Exposure
Customers of IDCF Cloud; IDC Frontier lists IDCF Cloud TypeS and its private-cloud offering as outside the incident (translated from Japanese) (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08). For any other body, the condition is a website, mail or form service whose hosting and recovery copies depend on one provider.
Defender takeaway
Check where the recovery copies of hosted websites, mail, forms and line-of-business systems live: IDC Frontier first expected restoration only from copies customers hold themselves (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-08), and its own snapshot backups became retrievable for 194 of the 495 customers only a week into the outage (IDC Frontier, 2026-10-14); the attacker's console message claims it wiped 554,153 snapshots, which the provider's report does not confirm (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-08). A copy in the provider's own environment is not one to count on for the recovery window.
Update16 Oct 2026 04:12 UTCrun 2026-10-16T0256Z-inteltitleheadlinesummarysourcesevidencesourcing_notebody

IDC Frontier's fifth report of 2026-10-14 says that, with an external security firm, it confirmed the backup data is safe, so the 194 of the 495 affected customers that used its snapshot function can retrieve it, and that it found no trace of customer data in the affected zones being queried or carried out, so it judges that none left those servers, while confirming improper queries of the registration data of 48 customers in its cloud portal with no trace of it being taken (translated from Japanese; IDC Frontier, 2026-10-14). This replaces the third report's expectation that data could be restored only from customers' own backups; the report does not state the intrusion route.

item.title: Lumen: a botnet takes its C2 address from a GitHub poem and spreads through exposed AI and developer servers
item.description: Lumen's Black Lotus Labs tracks PoeLLM, a financially motivated botnet active since at least April 2026 that Lumen says has impacted more than 3,400 servers, mostly in the United States and Western Europe, among them exposed LiteLLM, Ollama, Gotenberg and Gitea servers, with Ivanti Sentry possibly targeted. The malware derives its command-and-control address from words in a poem in a GitHub repository, runs XMRig and Iron miners and turns victims into scanners and exploit launchers that Lumen says likely abuse the LiteLLM CVE-2026-42271 path.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB2

PoeLLM: a cryptomining botnet that reads its C2 address out of a GitHub poem compromises exposed LiteLLM, Ollama, Gotenberg and Gitea servers and turns them into scanners

Lumen's Black Lotus Labs says PoeLLM has been active since at least April 2026, deploys XMRig and Iron cryptocurrency miners that connect to a Kryptex mining pool, and is deployed through vulnerability exploitation of publicly exposed services, mainly LiteLLM and Ollama and, in the hundreds, the Gotenberg PDF converter and Gitea, with other products such as Ivanti Sentry possibly targeted (Lumen, 2026-10-07). It counts more than 3,400 impacted servers, a figure it raised after first circulating the report (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-07), predominantly in the United States and Western Europe, and assesses that PoeLLM is associated with an Italian-speaking threat actor (Lumen, 2026-10-07).

The command channel is the unusual part: the malware derives its current C2 server from keywords in a poem hosted in a GitHub repository, so the operator rotates servers by editing the poem, which Lumen counts 11 edits of since the first commit on 2026-04-13 (Lumen, 2026-10-07). Several C2 servers were routers with exposed administration pages, which Lumen reads as the operator repurposing compromised routers (Lumen, 2026-10-07). Infected servers become scanners and exploit launchers that sweep ports 3000 and 4000, the primary ports of Gotenberg and LiteLLM, and send a crafted POST that makes the target fetch a payload from the C2; the payload is a single ELF binary that bundles a remote shell, the miners, HTTP and HTTPS scanning and exploit deployment, and beacons back to the C2 (Lumen, 2026-10-07). For LiteLLM, Lumen says the endpoint /mcp-rest/test/connection, which the CVE-2026-42271 command injection references, was likely the exploitation path (Lumen, 2026-10-07), and BleepingComputer adds that Horizon3 showed it can be chained with CVE-2026-48710 for unauthenticated remote code execution (BleepingComputer, 2026-10-07). Lumen met the infrastructure while investigating the Ivanti Sentry flaw CVE-2026-10520, when a compromised Sentry victim contacted a PoeLLM C2 and began scanning for other vulnerable devices; it states no further link between that flaw and the botnet (Lumen, 2026-10-07).

Exposure
Internet-reachable LiteLLM, Gotenberg, Ollama and Gitea servers, and Ivanti Sentry on a vulnerable build; Gotenberg's own installation guidance warns against exposing the service to the internet (Lumen, 2026-10-07). An external attack-surface scan plus the patch level of LiteLLM (CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710) and Sentry (CVE-2026-10520) shows whether a host is in scope.
Detection
Egress telemetry from AI, PDF-conversion and Git servers to mining pools and to unfamiliar C2 addresses, servers originating scans toward ports 3000 and 4000, and process telemetry for an unfamiliar ELF binary running on such servers (Lumen, 2026-10-07). Patching removes the entry point, not a running implant, so hosts that were exposed on a vulnerable build need the check as well.
Defender takeaway
Bring AI gateways and utility services such as these into the same exposure and patch inventory as other internet-facing software, take them off the internet where they need no public reach, and check any host that was exposed on a vulnerable build for miners and outbound scan traffic, since Lumen reports that infected servers are reused to attack others.

item.title: Registry-level DNS hijacks of .gh, .sl and .as produced valid HTTPS certificates for Google names
item.description: Google's Chrome team reported on 2026-10-06 that attackers compromised the .gh, .sl and .as country-code registries, changed authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates for Google domains and for domains of other organizations; Chrome blocked them and Google had the issuing authorities revoke the Google certificates. Google names no attacker or entry vector and says it cannot guarantee it found every affected domain; The Hacker News found 12 certificates for Google and YouTube names in public logs, 11 issued by Let's Encrypt and one by ZeroSSL, first logged between 2026-09-22 and 2026-09-27.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

Attackers compromised the .gh, .sl and .as country-code registries, rewrote authoritative DNS and obtained valid HTTPS certificates for Google and YouTube names

Google's Chrome Secure Web and Networking Team says attackers compromised the third-party .gh (Ghana), .sl (Sierra Leone) and .as (American Samoa) country-code top-level domains, modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains and domains of other organizations (Google, 2026-10-06). A certificate authority issues a domain-validated certificate once the applicant shows control of the domain, for example by adding a record to its DNS, so control of the registry's DNS passes that check; Google has no reason to believe the issuing authorities did anything wrong (The Hacker News, 2026-10-08; Google, 2026-10-06). Chrome blocked the Google certificates through its CRLSets mechanism and Google had the authorities revoke them; Certificate Transparency data then surfaced further organizations, among them leading global brands, whose certificates Chrome also blocked (Google, 2026-10-06).

The Hacker News' own review of public logs found 12 certificates for seven Google and YouTube names, 11 issued by Let's Encrypt and one by ZeroSSL, first logged on 2026-09-22 (.gh), 2026-09-25 (.sl) and 2026-09-27 (.as) and revoked between 2026-09-26 and 2026-10-01 (The Hacker News, 2026-10-08), and a Let's Encrypt staff member confirmed that certificates for Google and YouTube were issued and revoked (Let's Encrypt community forum, 2026-10-07). Google's post does not name the attackers, say how the registries were compromised, or say whether any certificate was used to pose as a Google site or read users' data (The Hacker News, 2026-10-08), and it names only these three registries (Google, 2026-10-06).

Exposure
Any organization holding a name under .gh, .sl or .as, including parked or regional variants of a brand name, and in principle any name whose registry or DNS operator an attacker can reach, because domain-validated issuance trusts whoever controls the DNS. Google tells owners of such names to review recent Certificate Transparency entries for unexpected issuance (Google, 2026-10-06).
Detection
Certificate Transparency monitoring of every owned name, parked and foreign registrations included, is the near-real-time signal, because every certificate Chrome trusts by default must be disclosed in public logs (Google, 2026-10-06); compare each issuing authority and account with the certificate inventory. Because the hijacks worked by changing authoritative DNS records, unexpected changes to a name's delegation or records are the second signal. After DNS control returns, restrictive CAA records bound to specific ACME accounts and validation methods stop an attacker from reusing a cached domain-control check to mint further certificates; CAA cannot prevent issuance while the hijack is live (Google, 2026-10-06).

Triage: a valid, correctly chained certificate is no longer evidence that a site is genuine once registry DNS can be changed. In the logs The Hacker News reviewed, every other certificate for google.com.gh, google.sl and google.as came from Google's own authority, while the 12 unauthorized ones came from Let's Encrypt and ZeroSSL, so an issuing authority or account outside your inventory, especially several certificates for one registry's names logged within hours, is the discriminator (The Hacker News, 2026-10-08).

Defender takeaway
Put every domain you hold, including defensive and foreign registrations, under Certificate Transparency monitoring and bind issuance with CAA to your own ACME account and validation methods; Google says browser-side blocking should not be relied on to protect users and does not reliably protect clients other than Chrome (Google, 2026-10-06).

item.title: GhostAction: fake security workflows now harvest whole git histories; rotating Actions secrets is not enough
item.description: StepSecurity and Socket report that on 2026-10-08 the GhostAction campaign used the GitHub credentials of two open-source maintainers to commit a workflow disguised as a security audit straight to the default branch of 345 to 346 repositories, including one of an Uber-owned organisation, and that the workflow now sends the credentials found in the working tree and in the entire git history, besides the named Actions secrets, to a hardcoded address over plain HTTP. StepSecurity read a run log showing the exfiltration was acknowledged four seconds after the run started; no malicious package release from the stolen credentials has been seen yet.
item.content:encoded:
NOTABLENATOB1

GhostAction returns: stolen maintainer credentials push a fake security-audit workflow into the victims' own GitHub repositories, which now harvests credentials from the entire git history

StepSecurity reports that on 2026-10-08 the GhostAction GitHub Actions credential-theft campaign used the accounts of two open-source maintainers to push a workflow disguised as a security improvement to 345 repositories in two automated sweeps, among them an Uber-owned repository that one maintainer could still write to (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); Socket's independent analysis counts 346 (Socket, 2026-10-09). The operator holds a maintainer's GitHub credential, which StepSecurity assesses as most plausibly a personal access token leaked through infostealer logs or credential dumps, then commits a workflow titled to look like a security audit straight to the default branch under the victim's own identity, unsigned and without a pull request; that push runs it, and nothing in an audit log looks anomalous unless the content is read (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). GitGuardian says the technique was later reused in the Shai-Hulud campaigns and remains at the core of the Mini Shai-Hulud malware family (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

The newer payload sends the named Actions secrets and every cloud, AI-provider and SaaS credential pattern found in the working tree and the entire git history to a hardcoded address over plain HTTP, so no DNS lookup occurs (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). StepSecurity saw the attacker's server acknowledge the request four seconds into the run at the Uber-owned repository (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); neither it nor Socket has seen a malicious package release from the stolen credentials yet (Socket, 2026-10-09; StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). A Socket update line claims more than 500 accounts and tens of thousands of repositories since 7 October without a method, against 346 for the 8 October burst in its own body and 378 live-workflow repositories across all waves in StepSecurity's code search of 2026-10-09, so the larger figure stays unconfirmed (Socket, 2026-10-09; StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).

Exposure
Any GitHub account whose token or session credential has leaked, and every repository it can write to; StepSecurity says a workflow posing as a security audit or an Actions security workflow that appeared in a repository you maintain since 2026-08-31 means treat it as a confirmed breach (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).
Detection
Source-control audit logs: workflow files added straight to default branches without a pull request by a maintainer identity, unsigned commits landing in many repositories within minutes; an organisation-scoped code search with StepSecurity's published content-marker queries for security-themed workflow files (audit, check or Actions security); runner egress logs: an HTTP POST to a bare IP address with no preceding DNS lookup (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09). Removing the workflow does not undo the theft: StepSecurity says any secret ever committed to a repository must be treated as compromised, so treat each run as an exfiltration, scan the full history and rotate every credential found (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09); GitGuardian adds that the GitHub credential that allowed the injection must be revoked too, or someone else will reuse it (GitGuardian, 2026-10-07).

Triage: the audit-log pattern separates this from a team adding a scanning workflow: no pull request, unsigned commits across many repositories, and a manual dispatch right after creation (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).

Defender takeaway
Search the GitHub organisations your teams and suppliers administer for security-themed workflow files (audit, check or Actions security); on a hit revoke the committing credential and rotate everything in the repository's full history. StepSecurity saw requiring approval for workflow runs stop the exfiltration and names branch protection on .github/workflows so workflow changes need pull-request review (StepSecurity, 2026-10-09).
